edgeR functionality in edger.bp

Source: vignettes/edgeR-functionality.Rmd
edgeR-functionality.Rmd

edger.bp is a BPCells-backed implementation layer for selected edgeR workflows. The package aims to reproduce edgeR results for supported inputs while avoiding full dense materialization of large pseudobulk matrices.

It does not replace the edgeR statistical documentation. Use edgeR’s guidance to choose the model, contrast, test, and filtering strategy; use edger.bp when the same workflow needs BPCells-backed storage and blockwise execution.

Function Mapping

edger.bp has two layers. The high-level workflow functions run preparation, normalization, optional filtering, dispersion estimation when needed, and the final GLM test. The lower-level GLM functions assume those preparation steps have already been handled and run only the blockwise fitting/testing stage.

edgeR operation High-level workflow Lower-level function Notes
filterByExpr() bp_prepare_dge(filter = TRUE) bp_filter_by_expr() Runs on BPCells-backed counts.
normLibSizes(method = "TMM") bp_prepare_dge() bp_calc_norm_factors() TMM and none are supported.
DGEList() preparation bp_prepare_dge() none Returns filtered counts, library sizes, normalization factors, and offsets.
estimateDisp() bp_lrt(), bp_qlf(), or bp_treat() when dispersion = NULL bp_estimate_disp_stream() Main streamed estimator.
dense estimateDisp() oracle bp_lrt(), bp_qlf(), or bp_treat() with dispersion.method = "dense" bp_estimate_disp_dense() Intended for small-data checks.
glmFit() + glmLRT() bp_lrt() bp_glm_lrt() Supports coefficient and contrast tests.
glmQLFit() + glmQLFTest() bp_qlf() bp_glm_qlf() Modern QL is the default; legacy QL is available.
glmQLFit() + glmTreat() bp_treat() bp_glm_treat() Modern Treat is the default; legacy Treat is available.

Choosing a Statistical Test

The package provides three test families and seven test configurations. The modern quasi-likelihood implementations are the defaults.

Test configuration Lower-level call Null hypothesis Reference distribution Multiple coefficients? Typical use
Likelihood-ratio test bp_glm_lrt() Selected coefficient(s) or contrast(s) equal zero Chi-squared Yes Fast testing when NB dispersions are treated as fixed.
Modern QLF bp_glm_qlf(..., legacy = FALSE) Selected coefficient(s) or contrast(s) equal zero Modern quasi-likelihood F Yes Recommended general-purpose differential-expression test.
Legacy QLF bp_glm_qlf(..., legacy = TRUE) Selected coefficient(s) or contrast(s) equal zero Legacy quasi-likelihood F Yes Compatibility with older edgeR QL workflows.
Modern Treat, interval null bp_glm_treat(..., legacy = FALSE, null = "interval") Absolute log2 fold change is no larger than lfc Modern QL threshold test One contrast Recommended when a minimum biologically relevant effect is required.
Modern Treat, worst-case null bp_glm_treat(..., legacy = FALSE, null = "worst.case") Threshold null evaluated at its least-favourable boundary Modern QL threshold test One contrast More conservative threshold formulation.
Legacy Treat, interval null bp_glm_treat(..., legacy = TRUE, null = "interval") Absolute log2 fold change is no larger than lfc Legacy QL threshold test One contrast Threshold testing compatible with older edgeR QL workflows.
Legacy Treat, worst-case null bp_glm_treat(..., legacy = TRUE, null = "worst.case") Threshold null evaluated at its least-favourable boundary Legacy QL threshold test One contrast Conservative threshold testing with legacy QL semantics.

Each family has a lower-level fitting/testing function and an end-to-end workflow:

Test family Lower-level function End-to-end workflow
LRT bp_glm_lrt() bp_lrt()
QLF bp_glm_qlf() bp_qlf()
Treat bp_glm_treat() bp_treat()

The lower-level functions require a design, dispersions, and offsets or library sizes. The end-to-end workflows can also filter genes, calculate TMM normalization factors, and estimate dispersions. Select legacy QL semantics in the high-level workflows through qlf.args or treat.args:

bp_qlf(
    y,
    design = design,
    group = group,
    coef = 2,
    qlf.args = list(legacy = TRUE)
)

bp_treat(
    y,
    design = design,
    group = group,
    coef = 2,
    lfc = log2(1.2),
    null = "interval",
    treat.args = list(legacy = TRUE)
)

The default Treat threshold is log2(1.2). Setting lfc = 0 delegates to the corresponding QLF test. Treat tests one coefficient or one contrast; LRT and QLF also support joint tests of multiple coefficients or contrast columns.

As a practical starting point, use modern QLF for a zero-effect primary analysis, modern Treat when the scientific question includes a minimum effect size, and LRT when speed or exploratory sensitivity is the priority. Legacy QLF and Treat are primarily compatibility and sensitivity-analysis paths.

In most analyses, start with a high-level workflow:

bp_lrt(y, design = design, group = group, coef = "groupB")
bp_qlf(y, design = design, group = group, coef = "groupB")
bp_treat(y, design = design, group = group, coef = "groupB")

These calls correspond to the usual native edgeR sequence of constructing a DGEList, filtering, normalizing, estimating dispersions, fitting a GLM, and testing a coefficient or contrast.

Use the lower-level functions when you want explicit control over intermediate objects. Common reasons are to reuse one prepared matrix, supply a dispersion vector estimated elsewhere, compare one stage directly with native edgeR, or avoid repeating preparation inside a loop.

For example, the high-level call:

bp_lrt(y, design = design, group = group, coef = "groupB")

is roughly equivalent to:

prep <- bp_prepare_dge(y, design = design, group = group)
disp <- bp_estimate_disp_stream(
    prep$counts,
    design = design,
    group = group,
    lib.size = prep$effective.lib.size,
    offset = prep$offset
)

lrt <- bp_glm_lrt(
    prep$counts,
    design = design,
    dispersion = disp$tagwise.dispersion,
    offset = prep$offset,
    coef = "groupB"
)

The same relationship holds for bp_qlf() versus bp_glm_qlf(), and bp_treat() versus bp_glm_treat().

Supported Scope

The audited path covers non-negative count matrices with genes as rows and samples or pseudobulk columns as columns. The current package focuses on:

  • TMM normalization or no normalization;
  • edgeR-compatible expression filtering;
  • common, trended, and tagwise dispersion estimation;
  • coefficient and contrast tests;
  • LRT, modern QLF, legacy QLF, modern Treat, and legacy Treat;
  • scalar or gene-level supplied dispersions;
  • sample-level offsets represented as a vector, or row-constant offset matrices.

The following edgeR features are not part of the supported path unless they are separately audited and tested:

  • robust dispersion or robust QL estimation;
  • observation weights;
  • gene-specific offset matrices;
  • normalization methods other than TMM and none;
  • exact compatibility with edgeR versions outside the audited dependency stacks.

Check the audited versions with:

library(edger.bp)

bp_check_versions(error = FALSE)
#>   package installed expected version_supported   ok     stack
#> 1       R     4.5.3    4.5.3              TRUE TRUE conda-r45
#> 2   edgeR     4.8.2    4.8.2              TRUE TRUE conda-r45
#> 3   limma    3.66.0   3.66.0              TRUE TRUE conda-r45
#> 4 BPCells     0.3.1    0.3.1              TRUE TRUE conda-r45

Native edgeR and edger.bp Side by Side

This small example runs the same two-group workflow with native edgeR and edger.bp.

library(edgeR)
library(BPCells)
library(Matrix)

set.seed(48)

ngenes <- 115L
nsamples <- 6L
group <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3L))
design <- model.matrix(~ group)

base_mean <- rgamma(ngenes, shape = 2, rate = 0.2)
counts <- vapply(seq_len(nsamples), function(j) {
    as.integer(rnbinom(ngenes, mu = base_mean, size = 4))
}, integer(ngenes))

counts[sample(length(counts), size = floor(length(counts) * 0.35))] <- 0L
counts[1:3, ] <- 0L

rownames(counts) <- paste0("gene", seq_len(ngenes))
colnames(counts) <- paste0("sample", seq_len(nsamples))

bp_dir <- tempfile("edger-bp-functionality-")
bp_counts <- BPCells::write_matrix_dir(
    BPCells::convert_matrix_type(Matrix(counts, sparse = TRUE), "uint32_t"),
    dir = bp_dir
)

The native edgeR workflow is:

dge <- DGEList(counts)
keep <- filterByExpr(dge, design = design, group = group)
dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
dge <- normLibSizes(dge)
dge <- estimateDisp(dge, design = design)

fit_lrt <- glmFit(dge, design = design)
edge_lrt <- glmLRT(fit_lrt, coef = 2)

fit_ql <- glmQLFit(
    dge,
    design = design,
    dispersion = dge$tagwise.dispersion,
    legacy = FALSE
)
edge_qlf <- glmQLFTest(fit_ql, coef = 2)
edge_treat <- glmTreat(fit_ql, coef = 2)

The corresponding high-level edger.bp calls are:

bp_lrt_fit <- bp_lrt(
    bp_counts,
    design = design,
    group = group,
    coef = 2,
    block.size = 10L,
    workers = 1L
)

bp_qlf_fit <- bp_qlf(
    bp_counts,
    design = design,
    group = group,
    coef = 2,
    block.size = 10L,
    workers = 1L
)

bp_treat_fit <- bp_treat(
    bp_counts,
    design = design,
    group = group,
    coef = 2,
    block.size = 10L,
    workers = 1L
)

A compact numerical comparison:

max_abs_diff <- function(x, y) {
    max(abs(x - y), na.rm = TRUE)
}

comparison <- data.frame(
    quantity = c(
        "filter keep vector",
        "TMM norm factors",
        "tagwise dispersion",
        "LRT p-values",
        "modern QLF p-values",
        "modern Treat p-values"
    ),
    max_abs_diff = c(
        max_abs_diff(as.integer(bp_lrt_fit$prepare$keep), as.integer(keep)),
        max_abs_diff(bp_lrt_fit$prepare$norm.factors, dge$samples$norm.factors),
        max_abs_diff(bp_lrt_fit$dispersion$tagwise.dispersion, dge$tagwise.dispersion),
        max_abs_diff(bp_lrt_fit$lrt$table$PValue, edge_lrt$table$PValue),
        max_abs_diff(bp_qlf_fit$qlf$table$PValue, edge_qlf$table$PValue),
        max_abs_diff(bp_treat_fit$treat$table$PValue, edge_treat$table$PValue)
    )
)
knitr::kable(
    transform(comparison, max_abs_diff = formatC(max_abs_diff, format = "e", digits = 2))
)
quantity max_abs_diff
filter keep vector 0.00e+00
TMM norm factors 0.00e+00
tagwise dispersion 0.00e+00
LRT p-values 0.00e+00
modern QLF p-values 1.52e-13
modern Treat p-values 1.16e-13

These comparisons are the package’s main correctness target: for supported inputs, the BPCells-backed workflow should match the corresponding native edgeR workflow to numerical tolerance.

Coefficients, Contrasts, and Marker Designs

coef and contrast follow edgeR conventions. Coefficients can be selected by index or by design column name:

bp_lrt(bp_counts, design = design, group = group, coef = "groupB")

contrast <- c("(Intercept)" = 0, "groupB" = 1)
bp_lrt(bp_counts, design = design, group = group, contrast = contrast)

For marker testing, a binary one-vs-rest design and a multi-cluster contrast design answer related but different questions:

# Binary one-vs-rest: selected cluster against all other columns pooled together.
selected <- col_data$cluster == "cl01"
design_binary <- model.matrix(~ selected)
bp_treat(bp_counts, design = design_binary, group = selected, coef = "selectedTRUE")

# Multi-cluster contrasts: one shared model with explicit cluster contrasts.
cluster <- factor(col_data$cluster)
design_cluster <- model.matrix(~ 0 + cluster)
contrast_cl01 <- rep(-1 / (nlevels(cluster) - 1), nlevels(cluster))
names(contrast_cl01) <- colnames(design_cluster)
contrast_cl01["clustercl01"] <- 1
bp_treat(bp_counts, design = design_cluster, group = cluster, contrast = contrast_cl01)

The second pattern can be faster for many clusters because the QL fit can be shared, but it changes the estimand. Choose the design for the scientific question first, then tune the implementation.

Runtime Controls

edger.bp materializes blocks of genes for edgeR GLM fitting. The main controls are:

  • block.size: larger blocks reduce overhead but increase memory per worker;
  • workers: parallel row-block workers for supported stages;
  • BPCells storage order: column-ordered matrices are efficient for sample-wise operations, while row-ordered companions can help gene-block operations.

For full pseudobulk datasets, use Slurm rather than an interactive session and record the package versions, design matrix, contrast, block.size, workers, and peak memory.
